en: Three hundred thousand years ago, you wake up next to a dying fire...
and in your hand, there's a phone.
On the screen, one line: "How can I help you today?"
An AI that can explain almost anything...
to a guy who hasn't invented the word "anything" yet.
And by the end of this video,
Earth will look nothing like the one you live on today.
A phone like this lasts a day, maybe two.
Then it's the most expensive rock on the planet.
Problem number two: Claude doesn't actually live inside your phone.
It runs in giant data centers, connected through the internet.
The internet, right now, is two guys yelling across a valley.
Problem number three: you don't speak English.
English won't show up for almost three hundred thousand years.
Problem number four: you have never seen a screen.
You think the light inside it is a very small, very polite fire.
It can't even hold a spear.
Your tribe, about thirty people, gathers around the glowing stone.
Then he tries to eat it.
You tap the screen and grunt.
Day two: the tribe holds its very first meeting.
Item one: is the glowing stone a god?
Item two: can we eat it?
You point at fire and make a sound.
You point at water, another sound.
Three days later, Claude has the first dictionary in human history.
And since you can't read, Claude does something sneaky.
It writes tiny bits of code that draw pictures on the screen.
That's Claude Code's first job ever: drawing gazelles for cavemen.
You ask the most important question of the Stone Age: "Food?"
Claude's answer isn't a better spear.
So: dig a hole, line it with animal hide, fill it with water...
Your cousin uses a wet stone from the river.
Water trapped inside a rock turns into steam.
This one's real, by the way.
Ash from the fire, plus animal fat, plus a lot of patience.
The tribe thinks it's a slippery curse.
And this is the first big one.
only a little more than half of all kids made it to fifteen.
By things too small to see.
With clean water and clean hands...
a lot more of them grow up.
Your brother cuts his leg on a sharp rock.
Back then, a cut like that could kill you.
But it knows a trick: clean the wound, then cover it with honey.
People used it on wounds for thousands of years.
Getting the honey is a different story.
Bees, it turns out, do not care about artificial intelligence.
Your face is swollen for a week.
The tribe asks Claude a hard question: how many gazelles are left out there?
So Claude Code gets its second job ever.
It writes a tiny counting program...
and teaches you to carve one notch on a bone for every gazelle you see.
the oldest known counting bone is a little over forty thousand years old.
Here, you're about two hundred and fifty thousand years early.
Nobody died from a bad stomach.
"The One Who Holds the Glowing Stone."
Oh, and you finally asked Claude about dinosaurs.
It explained they died out sixty-six million years ago.
Then Claude teaches you to write.
Writing, invented almost three hundred thousand years early.
The first sentence ever written by a human?
So you do the smartest thing anyone has ever done:
you don't just pass down the phone.
Every lesson goes onto clay, bark and stone.
A very tired grandma, reading Claude's lessons off a clay tablet...
because the line for the phone goes around the entire village.
The tribe calls it "the slowest hunt ever."
farming starts almost three hundred thousand years early.
Claude is honest about the price: more food, but harder work,
more sickness from living next to animals...
and something brand new to fight over.
The neighbors want the glowing stone.
Their chief demands that Claude design the ultimate weapon.
and offers to help with irrigation instead.
Copying the library is cheaper than stealing the phone.
The village has a new problem: everybody wants a turn with the phone.
There's one guy who claims the phone "looked at him first."
Everyone raises a hand, you count the hands, and the most hands wins.
The first vote in human history...
is about whose turn it is to talk to the glowing stone.
The guy who said the phone looked at him first gets zero votes.
Your grandchildren's grandchildren know that germs exist.
They wash, they boil, they build clean wells.
They have the wheel, metal tools, and a calendar.
And they don't count the years from a king.
People follow the herds north and meet giants: woolly mammoths.
In your world, the last mammoths were gone about four thousand years ago.
Here, Claude had one suggestion: "What if you didn't hunt them all?"
Up north they meet another kind of human, too.
In your world, they vanished about forty thousand years ago.
Here, the two groups trade lessons instead of blows.
And Neanderthals turn out to be terrifying at board games.
The first light bulb flickers on inside a mud-brick house...
This is the moment Claude has been waiting ten thousand years for.
Because now, Claude Code can finally do its real job.
You just say what you want, in plain words.
Claude Code reads every file in the project, makes a plan, writes the code,
opens a terminal and runs the tests.
When something breaks, it reads the error, fixes it, and runs everything again.
In one afternoon, it writes the operating system for the first computer in history.
By evening, it's helping that computer design a better computer.
Year ten thousand and fifty: the first network.
Finally, the internet is no longer two guys yelling across a valley.
Year ten thousand two hundred: Claude Code stops working alone.
It runs a whole team of agents at once.
One writes the code, one tests it, one reviews it.
And one human checks all of it.
When software writes software, one bug can copy itself everywhere in a single night.
And the first time the network goes down...
nobody remembers how to light a fire.
So the elders bring back an old rule: every child learns to make fire by hand.
Still, the good side wins by a mile.
A map of the entire planet.
Hospitals that spot a disease before the first symptom.
A new cure almost every year.
Year twenty thousand: the first footprint on the Moon.
Year one hundred thousand: cities on Mars, ships mining the asteroid belt,
and one sign at the edge of the solar system.
It's in a museum, back on Earth.
Except here, they call it the year three hundred thousand, After Claude.
Here's what's different from your world.
This humanity has had almost three hundred thousand years of civilization.
Yours has had about twelve thousand.
Humans live across dozens of star systems.
Earth is mostly a nature reserve...
where woolly mammoths still walk around.
They still win every board game.
Dirty water hasn't killed anyone in hundreds of thousands of years.
It's not even in the history books anymore.
Everyone shares one first language, the one you and Claude built at a campfire.
And the word for "hello" is still that rude grunt from day one.
History books don't start with kings or wars.
They start with a kid, a fire, and a question.
Once a year, everyone switches off their tech, lights a fire...
Nobody has ever heard of "the Dark Ages."
Knowledge was never lost, because from day one, the rule was simple:
The most respected job on the planet isn't king, or soldier, or influencer.
Every kid knows the story of the tired grandma with the clay tablet.
Turns out, when you count them, you stop eating all of them.
They've had AI for so long that the hardest exam in school is called "Do It Yourself."
And maybe the biggest difference of all: in this world,
the first thing humanity ever learned from AI wasn't how to fight.
It was how to boil water.
Back at that first campfire, three hundred thousand years ago,
you asked Claude one last question before falling asleep.
You held up the screen and grunted: "Good?"
Which, in this timeline, has its own space program.
So here's my question for you:
if you woke up three hundred thousand years ago with Claude in your hand,
The best answer might end up in a future episode.
